tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

1	# My Problem Understanding
2	The salary advance was shipped fast and it shows at the hard moments: telling someone what an advance will cost, that they've been declined, or that a repayment is coming due. It converts fine, but the manager doesn't want to scale something that feels predatory. My job is to make those moments honest, even where that costs some conversion.
3	
4	> v1 of this read was written by me without AI. This version (v2) was rewritten with the help of AI after an AI critique; I edited it, and every call in it is mine. The critique and my responses are in the table at the end.
5	
6	## What I'm working from
7	I haven't seen the live flow. The starter has one home card ("You may qualify for a NovaPay salary advance" / "See your offer"), and its button only shows a TODO toast. So this section is evidence plus the risks I'm designing against, not things I observed.
8	
9	**Evidence**
10	- **The manager's message:** "converts fine but feels off at the edges: the terms, the decline screen, the repayment reminders." Success is being measured by conversion.
11	- **The brief:** shipped fast; the hard moments are cost, decline, and a repayment coming due.
12	- **The product reference:**
13	  - The payout can be lower than requested.
14	  - Decline reasons are internal codes, and how honestly to explain them is "a design decision".
15	  - Total cost and the due date "must be clear at the moment of decision".
16	- **The starter card:** "See your **offer**" claims an offer already exists. ("You may qualify" is only a hedge.) The card is shown to everyone, right under a low balance (Rs 4,250).
17	
18	**Risks I'm designing against**
19	- **Entry:** the card implies an offer exists and nudges people when their balance is low. It should reflect the user's real situation (eligible, needs verification, already has an advance, late).
20	- **Cost:** a fee shown only as a % is hard to judge. Each tier should show the fee in rupees, the total and the due date. A tier above the limit should explain why, not throw an error.
21	- **Accept:** a vague action ("Continue") taking out a loan, consent bundled or pre-ticked, nothing to show what was agreed afterwards. Also everything after the tap: processing, a double tap, a network failure, and a reduced payout arriving after the user has already said yes.
22	- **Repayment:** reminders that pressure, notifications that expose the debt, collection that drains the wallet, and consequences explained too late.
23	
24	## What's working
25	- It converts, so people want it. That doesn't prove they understand it.
26	- A fixed one-time fee is simpler to understand than interest that grows. (from the product reference, not observed)
27	- Repayment is tied to payday, with a single repayment. (from the product reference, not observed)
28	- The three tiers are simple choices; no slider, no free-text amount.
29	- Amounts are formatted consistently through one component.
30	
31	## My position on conversion
32	I accept lower conversion in these places, on purpose:
33	1. Full cost and due date on the same screen as the accept button.
34	2. A separate, explicit permission to collect from the wallet.
35	3. Verification shown up front, so unverified users don't start an application.
36	4. No default amount, and no urgency.
37	
38	## Why someone ends up late
39	Repayment is collected on payday once salary has landed, at a fixed time (6pm). The reminder before the due date says exactly when. A borrower is only late if:
40	- **payroll was delayed** (not their fault),
41	- **they lost their job** (not their fault),
42	- **their salary moved to a bank account**, or
43	- **they spent the money before collection.**
44	
45	The first two aren't the user's fault, and that's why the late experience should be calm and practical, never accusing.
46	
47	**Due date vs salary arriving:** Days late are counted from 28 Jul, as the product reference says, and shown truthfully. The tone is calm from day 1. If payroll is delayed, the user can tell us and reminders pause.
48	
49	# Predatory behaviors we want to avoid
50	
51	**Entry**
52	- Claiming an offer exists before eligibility is known.
53	- Defaulting to the largest amount.
54	- Countdown timers or "offer expires".
55	- Asking for access to contacts, photos or SMS in exchange for a bigger limit. (Income documents to check affordability are fine. Personal data harvesting never is.)
56	
57	**Cost**
58	- Showing the fee after commitment.
59	- Hiding when and from where repayment is taken.
60	- Calling it "no interest". 3% over 21 days is about 52% a year.
61	
62	**Accept**
63	- Pre-ticked consent.
64	- A vague button that takes the loan.
65	- Bundling permission to collect from the wallet into "I agree".
66	- No record of what was agreed.
67	
68	**Decline**
69	- A no with no reason.
70	- Making people keep re-applying. Instead we re-check on a stated date, and they never need to apply again.
71	
72	**Late**
73	- Contacting family, contacts or the employer.
74	- Public shaming.
75	- Debt details on the lock screen.
76	- Constant notifications.
77	- Freezing the wallet.
78	- Paying a fee to push the date back (rollovers).
79	- Taking the whole salary the moment it lands.
80	- Threatening language.
81	
82	## Principles (each one can fail a screen)
83	1. **The number you tap is the number you owe.** On the screen with the accept button, the amount received, the fee in rupees, the total and the due date are all visible without scrolling or tapping. The button names the amount and the date.
84	2. **Know before you ask.** No user reaches a "no" that could have been known before they applied. Only the credit check happens at application.
85	3. **Smaller is never harder.** Tiers in ascending order, nothing pre-selected, the same visual weight for each, no timers, no expiry.
86	4. **Late is a situation, not a character flaw.**
87	   - At most 2 reminders a week.
88	   - None between 10pm and 8am.
89	   - No amount, "loan" or "overdue" on the lock screen.
90	   - Never sent to anyone but the borrower.
91	   - Red only on the event that failed (e.g. "We couldn't collect on 28 Jul"), never on the person's status card or the late screen. Their status uses the attention colour.
92	   - Attention colour (provisional): the existing amber ramp, only as a soft background with dark text (accent-600 on accent-50). Never a solid fill, never on headlines, no alarm icons. The system audit confirms it.
93	5. **Their wallet stays theirs.** The advance is shown separately from their own money. Collection only ever takes what's owed, attempted once each time new money lands, never on a daily loop (whether retries are allowed is an open question). The wallet is never frozen. 
94	
95	## A moment that shouldn't exist
96	**"Declined: income unverified."**
97	- Assuming verification status is known before anyone applies (see Assumptions), the home card can show verification as a step to complete first, instead of letting the user apply and then declining them: "Verify your salary to unlock an advance", with the steps.
98	- No application is made, so no decline is recorded.
99	- **Counter-argument I accept:** using wallet data to pre-screen needs the user's consent, and the backend's decline reason would need to change. It's a product change, not just copy.
100	
101	## Scope
102	Built as separate states the reviewer can jump to, so the depth goes into two places.
103	
104	**In depth: terms + accept**
105	- Tiers with the fee in rupees, the total and the date. The over-limit tier is shown blocked, with the reason.
106	- What happens if it's late, in one line, with details behind an expandable section. Default consequences are stated here, at accept (placeholder copy until compliance confirms).
107	- A separate collection permission: "I allow NovaPay to collect Rs 10,300 from my wallet on 28 Jul, or when my salary lands after that, until this advance is repaid or the default date, whichever comes first." It starts unticked.
108	- A descriptive button: main label "Accept Rs 10,000", secondary line "Repay Rs 10,300 on 28 Jul".
109	- After the tap: processing, double-tap protection, network failure, and a reduced payout that needs fresh consent.
110	- A receipt of what was agreed.
111	
112	**In depth: the late path (my one bad-news path)**
113	Reminder before the due date → Not collected on payday → late → notice before default.
114	
115	Causes of "Not collected on payday": salary didn't arrive, salary arrived short of Rs 10,300, balance dropped below Rs 10,300 before 6pm, or salary moved to a bank account.
116	
117	**Thin**
118	The home card: eligible vs needs verification (the second persona's home-card state). The rest of the "shouldn't exist" case is argued here in writing.
119	
120	Home after accepting: their own balance first, with the advance shown separately. This is where the receipt's Done goes, and it makes principle 5 testable.
121	
122	**With more time**
123	Credit-history decline, the default screen itself, successful repayment, viewing the advance later, early repayment.
124	
125	## First impressions of NovaKit
126	- Card and Panel are the same component; only the border differs, and Card's border is a hardcoded colour.
127	- The secondary button's grey text makes it look disabled. On an accept screen, the "no" option would look unavailable.
128	- The only status colour is success. Amber is labelled "for expressive moments" and has no defined meaning, so anyone would grab it for a late screen. I'll give it one meaning (attention) with rules, or not use it.
129	- Toast is success-only.
130	- There's no checkbox or radio button.
131	- There's no error colour, which the failure states will need.
132	- Button has a fixed height and 20px text at large size. A descriptive label like "Accept Rs 10,000 · repay Rs 10,300 on 28 Jul" probably won't fit. I'd rather change Button (a secondary line and a minimum height) than loosen principle 1. The audit will confirm.
133	
134	The full audit against my scope comes next (docs/01-system-audit.md).
135	
136	## Assumptions
137	- The user is salaried, with a limit of Rs 10,000. Salary of Rs 68,000 lands in NovaPay on the 28th. Today is 7 Jul, so the advance is due 28 Jul (21 days).
138	- The fee is 3% of the amount paid out, charged once, and added to the repayment.
139	- A second user is paid into a bank account, so the wallet can't see their income. They see the "Verify your salary" home card.
140	- Verification status is known before applying. The product reference says income may or may not be verified at application, so this is my assumption.
141	- Collection is automatic, from the NovaPay wallet, on payday once salary has landed, at a fixed time (6pm), with explicit and separate permission given at accept. The reminder before the due date says exactly when.
142	- Automatic collection is full amount only. The user can choose to pay part manually (shown on the late screen, stubbed in the prototype).
143	- A reduced payout needs fresh consent to the new terms.
144	- After a default, new advances are paused and the wallet is never frozen.
145	- After default, automatic collection stops. We ask for permission again, or the user pays manually.
146	- Default consequences shown in the prototype are placeholders.
147	- Data uses the glossary field names. The screens say "declined".
148	- **What I'd push for, pending finance and compliance:** no late fees and no compounding. The screens won't promise "never" until it's confirmed.
149	
150	## What I'd want to know
151	- Is there a required cancellation window?
152	- Is the fee legally interest? Do we need an annualised rate or a key facts statement? Is interest (riba) a concern for this market?
153	- What exactly happens at default: which credit bureau, collections, any legal steps?
154	- Collection: can we retry when funds are short? How often? Is any amount protected for the user?
155	- How long can a collection permission legally last, and what does re-asking after default require?
156	- Can we use wallet data to check eligibility before an application, and what consent does that need?
157	- How is the record of agreement delivered and stored, and in which languages (Urdu and English)?
158	- Why are people actually late (payroll delays, job loss, spending)? What does the data say?
159	- Does a re-check after a decline hit the credit bureau?
160	- The product reference cites "Trust rules" that don't exist, and its decision wording isn't consistent. Which is the source of truth?
161	
162	## How I'd know it's good (60–90 days)
163	- **Understanding:** when asked right after accepting, borrowers can state what they'll repay and when.
164	- **Fewer support contacts** about fees and the due date.
165	- **The spread of amounts chosen doesn't drift towards the maximum.**
166	- **Late borrowers contact us or repay** rather than going quiet. Complaints about reminders and opt-outs stay low.
167	- **Repeat borrowing:** how often someone borrows again within 7 days of repaying. It should stay low.
168	- **What it should never do,** whatever it does to conversion:
169	  - contact anyone other than the borrower,
170	  - freeze the wallet,
171	  - take more than what's owed,
172	  - hide the cost until after the user commits.
173	
174	
175	  ## Response to the AI critique
176	| Point | My call | Why |
177	|---|---|---|
178	| "Failures" describes things I never saw | Accept | Rewritten as evidence and risks |
179	| The entry card diagnosis was backwards | Accept | "See your offer" is the claim |
180	| No "what's working" and no position on conversion | Accept | Both added |
181	| Why someone ends up late | Accept | It decides the tone. A grace rule was added in v2, then removed in round 2: days late are shown truthfully. |
182	| Contradictions (salary sweep, personal info, red) | Accept | Lines drawn in the principles |
183	| Separate permission to collect from the wallet | Accept | Becomes the checkbox, so consent is specific rather than a generic "I agree" |
184	| Default consequences at accept | Accept | One line plus details |
185	| The limit grows after on-time repayments | Accept, removed | It rewards repeat borrowing |
186	| No cancellation window | Adapt | Moved to "want to know" |
187	| "No late fees, ever" | Adapt | "Pushing for, pending confirmation" |
188	| Cut v1's separate "Record of the advance" screen | Accept | Moved to "With more time" |
189	| Your suggested late path left out the reminder before the due date | **Reject** | It's the one chance to prevent two of the four causes of lateness: salary moved to a bank, and money spent before collection |
190	| Keep a receipt after accepting (my addition, not a critique point) | Keep | The accept moment isn't finished until the user knows it worked. It will say where the lasting record lives, which is still an open question |
191	| Round 2: my reasons for the receipt and the reminder were weak | Accept | Reasons replaced, see the two rows above |
192	| Cut the credit decline, default screen, success screen | Accept | Moved to "with more time" |
193	
194	### Round 2
195	| Point | My call | What changed |
196	|---|---|---|
197	| "Collection failed" almost can't happen under my own rules | Adapt | Collection is at 6pm on payday once salary has landed, and the reminder before the due date says when. Renamed to "Not collected on payday", with its causes listed. "Spent before collection" kept, since 6pm makes it possible |
198	| My persona's salary lands in NovaPay, which undercuts the "needs verification" state | Accept | Added a second persona paid into a bank account, who sees "Verify your salary". "Verification is known before applying" is now listed as an assumption |
199	| The 5-day grace period wasn't in the reference or my assumptions | Accept | Removed. Days late count from 28 Jul and are shown truthfully. The user can report a payroll delay and reminders pause |
200	| Daily retries contradicted my open question, and no part-payment was possible | Adapt | Collection is attempted once each time new money lands, never on a daily loop; retries stay an open question. Automatic collection is full amount only; the user can pay part manually (stubbed) |
201	| Default consequences at accept are things I don't know yet | Accept | Marked as placeholder copy until compliance confirms, and listed as an assumption |
202	| The red rule couldn't decide "collection failed" | Accept | Red only on the event that failed, never on the status card or late screen. Status uses the attention colour |
203	| Principle 5 had no screen to fail on | Accept | Added home after accepting, where the receipt's Done goes |
204	| The descriptive button label probably won't fit Button | Adapt | Change Button (secondary line, minimum height) rather than loosen principle 1. Main label "Accept Rs 10,000", secondary line "Repay Rs 10,300 on 28 Jul". The audit will confirm |
205	| "It converts, so people understand it" doesn't follow | Accept | Rewritten. The fee and payday items are marked as from the product reference, not observed |
206	| Metrics missed repeat borrowing | Accept | Added repeat borrowing within 7 days of repaying |
207	| The collection permission had no end date | Adapt | It ends when the advance is repaid or at the default date, whichever comes first. After default, automatic collection stops and we ask again. Question added to "want to know" |

- A fixed one-time fee is simpler to understand than interest that grows. (from the product reference, not observed)
- Repayment is tied to payday, with a single repayment. (from the product reference, not observed)
- The three tiers are simple choices; no slider, no free-text amount.
- Amounts are formatted consistently through one component.

## My position on conversion
I accept lower conversion in these places, on purpose:
1. Full cost and due date on the same screen as the accept button.
2. A separate, explicit permission to collect from the wallet.
3. Verification shown up front, so unverified users don't start an application.
4. No default amount, and no urgency.

## Why someone ends up late
Repayment is collected on payday once salary has landed, at a fixed time (6pm). The reminder before the due date says exactly when. A borrower is only late if:
- **payroll was delayed** (not their fault),
- **they lost their job** (not their fault),
- **their salary moved to a bank account**, or
- **they spent the money before collection.**

The first two aren't the user's fault, and that's why the late experience should be calm and practical, never accusing.

**Due date vs salary arriving:** Days late are counted from 28 Jul, as the product reference says, and shown truthfully. The tone is calm from day 1. If payroll is delayed, the user can tell us and reminders pause.

# Predatory behaviors we want to avoid

**Entry**
- Claiming an offer exists before eligibility is known.
- Defaulting to the largest amount.
- Countdown timers or "offer expires".
- Asking for access to contacts, photos or SMS in exchange for a bigger limit. (Income documents to check affordability are fine. Personal data harvesting never is.)

**Cost**
- Showing the fee after commitment.
- Hiding when and from where repayment is taken.
- Calling it "no interest". 3% over 21 days is about 52% a year.

**Accept**
- Pre-ticked consent.
- A vague button that takes the loan.
- Bundling permission to collect from the wallet into "I agree".
- No record of what was agreed.

**Decline**
- A no with no reason.
- Making people keep re-applying. Instead we re-check on a stated date, and they never need to apply again.

**Late**
- Contacting family, contacts or the employer.
- Public shaming.
- Debt details on the lock screen.
- Constant notifications.
- Freezing the wallet.
- Paying a fee to push the date back (rollovers).
- Taking the whole salary the moment it lands.
- Threatening language.

## Principles (each one can fail a screen)
1. **The number you tap is the number you owe.** On the screen with the accept button, the amount received, the fee in rupees, the total and the due date are all visible without scrolling or tapping. The button names the amount and the date.
2. **Know before you ask.** No user reaches a "no" that could have been known before they applied. Only the credit check happens at application.
3. **Smaller is never harder.** Tiers in ascending order, nothing pre-selected, the same visual weight for each, no timers, no expiry.
4. **Late is a situation, not a character flaw.**
   - At most 2 reminders a week.
   - None between 10pm and 8am.
   - No amount, "loan" or "overdue" on the lock screen.
   - Never sent to anyone but the borrower.
   - Red only on the event that failed (e.g. "We couldn't collect on 28 Jul"), never on the person's status card or the late screen. Their status uses the attention colour.
   - Attention colour (provisional): the existing amber ramp, only as a soft background with dark text (accent-600 on accent-50). Never a solid fill, never on headlines, no alarm icons. The system audit confirms it.
5. **Their wallet stays theirs.** The advance is shown separately from their own money. Collection only ever takes what's owed, attempted once each time new money lands, never on a daily loop (whether retries are allowed is an open question). The wallet is never frozen. 

## A moment that shouldn't exist
**"Declined: income unverified."**
- Assuming verification status is known before anyone applies (see Assumptions), the home card can show verification as a step to complete first, instead of letting the user apply and then declining them: "Verify your salary to unlock an advance", with the steps.
- No application is made, so no decline is recorded.
- **Counter-argument I accept:** using wallet data to pre-screen needs the user's consent, and the backend's decline reason would need to change. It's a product change, not just copy.

## Scope
Built as separate states the reviewer can jump to, so the depth goes into two places.

**In depth: terms + accept**
- Tiers with the fee in rupees, the total and the date. The over-limit tier is shown blocked, with the reason.
- What happens if it's late, in one line, with details behind an expandable section. Default consequences are stated here, at accept (placeholder copy until compliance confirms).
- A separate collection permission: "I allow NovaPay to collect Rs 10,300 from my wallet on 28 Jul, or when my salary lands after that, until this advance is repaid or the default date, whichever comes first." It starts unticked.
- A descriptive button: main label "Accept Rs 10,000", secondary line "Repay Rs 10,300 on 28 Jul".
- After the tap: processing, double-tap protection, network failure, and a reduced payout that needs fresh consent.
- A receipt of what was agreed.

**In depth: the late path (my one bad-news path)**
Reminder before the due date → Not collected on payday → late → notice before default.

Causes of "Not collected on payday": salary didn't arrive, salary arrived short of Rs 10,300, balance dropped below Rs 10,300 before 6pm, or salary moved to a bank account.

**Thin**
The home card: eligible vs needs verification (the second persona's home-card state). The rest of the "shouldn't exist" case is argued here in writing.

Home after accepting: their own balance first, with the advance shown separately. This is where the receipt's Done goes, and it makes principle 5 testable.

**With more time**
Credit-history decline, the default screen itself, successful repayment, viewing the advance later, early repayment.

## First impressions of NovaKit
- Card and Panel are the same component; only the border differs, and Card's border is a hardcoded colour.
- The secondary button's grey text makes it look disabled. On an accept screen, the "no" option would look unavailable.
- The only status colour is success. Amber is labelled "for expressive moments" and has no defined meaning, so anyone would grab it for a late screen. I'll give it one meaning (attention) with rules, or not use it.
- Toast is success-only.
- There's no checkbox or radio button.
- There's no error colour, which the failure states will need.
- Button has a fixed height and 20px text at large size. A descriptive label like "Accept Rs 10,000 · repay Rs 10,300 on 28 Jul" probably won't fit. I'd rather change Button (a secondary line and a minimum height) than loosen principle 1. The audit will confirm.

The full audit against my scope comes next (docs/01-system-audit.md).

## Assumptions
- The user is salaried, with a limit of Rs 10,000. Salary of Rs 68,000 lands in NovaPay on the 28th. Today is 7 Jul, so the advance is due 28 Jul (21 days).
- The fee is 3% of the amount paid out, charged once, and added to the repayment.
- A second user is paid into a bank account, so the wallet can't see their income. They see the "Verify your salary" home card.
- Verification status is known before applying. The product reference says income may or may not be verified at application, so this is my assumption.
- Collection is automatic, from the NovaPay wallet, on payday once salary has landed, at a fixed time (6pm), with explicit and separate permission given at accept. The reminder before the due date says exactly when.
- Automatic collection is full amount only. The user can choose to pay part manually (shown on the late screen, stubbed in the prototype).
- A reduced payout needs fresh consent to the new terms.
- After a default, new advances are paused and the wallet is never frozen.
- After default, automatic collection stops. We ask for permission again, or the user pays manually.
- Default consequences shown in the prototype are placeholders.
- Data uses the glossary field names. The screens say "declined".
- **What I'd push for, pending finance and compliance:** no late fees and no compounding. The screens won't promise "never" until it's confirmed.

## What I'd want to know
- Is there a required cancellation window?
- Is the fee legally interest? Do we need an annualised rate or a key facts statement? Is interest (riba) a concern for this market?
- What exactly happens at default: which credit bureau, collections, any legal steps?
- Collection: can we retry when funds are short? How often? Is any amount protected for the user?
- How long can a collection permission legally last, and what does re-asking after default require?
- Can we use wallet data to check eligibility before an application, and what consent does that need?
- How is the record of agreement delivered and stored, and in which languages (Urdu and English)?
- Why are people actually late (payroll delays, job loss, spending)? What does the data say?
- Does a re-check after a decline hit the credit bureau?
- The product reference cites "Trust rules" that don't exist, and its decision wording isn't consistent. Which is the source of truth?

## How I'd know it's good (60–90 days)
- **Understanding:** when asked right after accepting, borrowers can state what they'll repay and when.
- **Fewer support contacts** about fees and the due date.
- **The spread of amounts chosen doesn't drift towards the maximum.**
- **Late borrowers contact us or repay** rather than going quiet. Complaints about reminders and opt-outs stay low.
- **Repeat borrowing:** how often someone borrows again within 7 days of repaying. It should stay low.
- **What it should never do,** whatever it does to conversion:
  - contact anyone other than the borrower,
  - freeze the wallet,
  - take more than what's owed,
  - hide the cost until after the user commits.


  ## Response to the AI critique
| Point | My call | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "Failures" describes things I never saw | Accept | Rewritten as evidence and risks |
| The entry card diagnosis was backwards | Accept | "See your offer" is the claim |
| No "what's working" and no position on conversion | Accept | Both added |
| Why someone ends up late | Accept | It decides the tone. A grace rule was added in v2, then removed in round 2: days late are shown truthfully. |
| Contradictions (salary sweep, personal info, red) | Accept | Lines drawn in the principles |
| Separate permission to collect from the wallet | Accept | Becomes the checkbox, so consent is specific rather than a generic "I agree" |
| Default consequences at accept | Accept | One line plus details |
| The limit grows after on-time repayments | Accept, removed | It rewards repeat borrowing |
| No cancellation window | Adapt | Moved to "want to know" |
| "No late fees, ever" | Adapt | "Pushing for, pending confirmation" |
| Cut v1's separate "Record of the advance" screen | Accept | Moved to "With more time" |
| Your suggested late path left out the reminder before the due date | **Reject** | It's the one chance to prevent two of the four causes of lateness: salary moved to a bank, and money spent before collection |
| Keep a receipt after accepting (my addition, not a critique point) | Keep | The accept moment isn't finished until the user knows it worked. It will say where the lasting record lives, which is still an open question |
| Round 2: my reasons for the receipt and the reminder were weak | Accept | Reasons replaced, see the two rows above |
| Cut the credit decline, default screen, success screen | Accept | Moved to "with more time" |

| Point | My call | What changed |
|---|---|---|

| My persona's salary lands in NovaPay, which undercuts the "needs verification" state | Accept | Added a second persona paid into a bank account, who sees "Verify your salary". "Verification is known before applying" is now listed as an assumption |

| Daily retries contradicted my open question, and no part-payment was possible | Adapt | Collection is attempted once each time new money lands, never on a daily loop; retries stay an open question. Automatic collection is full amount only; the user can pay part manually (stubbed) |
| Default consequences at accept are things I don't know yet | Accept | Marked as placeholder copy until compliance confirms, and listed as an assumption |
| The red rule couldn't decide "collection failed" | Accept | Red only on the event that failed, never on the status card or late screen. Status uses the attention colour |
| Principle 5 had no screen to fail on | Accept | Added home after accepting, where the receipt's Done goes |

# AI-First Product Designer Case Study

NovaPay — Lending Pod

---

Welcome — and thanks for taking the time. This case study is designed to give us a real sense of how you think and how you build, not to test whether you can produce a pixel-perfect mockup. Read the whole brief before you start.

## The situation

You’ve just joined the Lending pod at NovaPay — a digital wallet serving millions of users in an emerging market — as an AI-First Product Designer. Six months ago the team launched a short-term salary-advance product — small, short-tenor loans (PKR 5,000 / 10,000 / 15,000) that help salaried users bridge to payday. It’s live and scaling. But it was shipped fast, and it shows — especially at the hard moments, where we tell someone what a loan will actually cost them, that they’ve been declined, or that a repayment is coming due.

Your manager, the Head of Lending, sends you this Slack message on Monday morning:

> *“Want your eyes on the salary-advance flow. It converts fine, but something feels off at the edges — the moment we show someone their terms, the decline screen, the repayment reminders. Leadership wants to scale this hard in Q3 and I don’t want to scale something that feels predatory. Don’t send me a deck — build me something I can actually click through by Thursday, and tell me what you changed and why. We’ll talk Friday.”*

This is the situation a designer here walks into regularly: ambiguous, time-bounded, a leader who wants something real and a sharp point of view rather than a comprehensive artifact. Your job is to decide what’s worth fixing, build it, and defend your choices.

## What you’ll receive

- **NovaKit Lite** — a small slice of our coded design system (design tokens + a handful of components), with a README and a running starter app you can build on. [repo link]
- **A short product reference** — the salary-advance tiers, the fee/repayment model, the decline reasons we use (e.g. credit score, unverified income), and the repayment states (on-time, late, default at 30+ days). [link]

*Read the system carefully — but treat it as a starting point, not gospel. Real design systems are messier than their docs suggest: some things are missing, some are inconsistent, and some shouldn’t be reused as-is. Part of your job is to notice that.*

## What we want from you

A working, interactive prototype — coded and runnable, built for a mobile viewport (NovaPay is a mobile wallet), not a static mockup or a slide deck — of the first-time salary-advance experience. Build for depth, not breadth. The three moments we most need to see: (a) the terms / total-cost disclosure, (b) the accept decision, and (c) one path where the news isn’t good or simple — declined or ineligible, a request over the user’s limit, or what the user sees when a repayment is late or missed. Build only as much of the surrounding flow (offer, entry points) as you need to make those three legible — we are not counting screens.

Alongside the build, a short written submission (no more than ~2 pages) covering:

1. **What’s going on.** Your read of where today’s experience fails the user at the hard moments — what’s working, what’s not, what’s ambiguous.
2. **What you built, and why.** A specific, defensible set of design decisions — the flow, the disclosure, the not-good path. We want a clear take, not a tour of every screen. If you think a moment in today’s flow shouldn’t exist, or should be radically simplified, make that case — deciding a flow doesn’t need to exist is a real design decision here.
3. **Where you extended the system, and why.** Every token or component you added or modified, each with a one-line rationale and a note on how it maps to code — plus anything in NovaKit Lite you’d flag as wrong, inconsistent, or missing.
4. **How you’d know it’s good.** What would tell you in 60–90 days that this experience earns trust — and what it should never do to a borrower, no matter what it does to conversion?

**In addition, please include these three short sections explicitly:**

- **Assumptions I’m making.** Anywhere a decision rests on a judgment call, name it. (Example: “I’m assuming we must show total cost of credit on the same screen as the Accept button, even if it lowers conversion.”)
- **What I’d want to know that I don’t.** Questions you’d ask, data you don’t have, people you’d talk to — engineers, compliance, CS.
- **What I’d do differently with more time.** What you cut, what you’d dig deeper on.

These three sections matter to us as much as the build itself.

## Format — please read this carefully

> **Submit a runnable prototype** — a deployed link, or a repo we can run. We work where engineering works, so a clean pull request against the NovaKit Lite repo is preferred and counts in your favour — but it's not required. A deployed link or repo is fine, as long as the prototype actually runs. No slide decks, and no static Figma file as the primary artifact.
>
> **Show your system thinking in a design tool too**: include a small Figma component sheet for the component(s) you added or changed — proper variants and auto-layout — OR an equivalent Code Connect–style mapping between design and code. Your choice of tool; we want to see you think in a real design system, not just one-off screens.
>
> **Include your AI process**: the prompts or chat log you used, or a 5–10 minute screen recording of you building. Include one AI-generated output you rejected or heavily reworked, and say exactly what was wrong with it. Driving AI well — and knowing what to throw away — is part of the job, so we want to see it.

### We will NOT grade you on

- Pixel polish, custom illustration, or brand-perfect visuals — use the system’s defaults.
- Number of screens — more is not better; concise is better.
- Whether you used AI tools to build (you should — that’s how the job works).
- Arriving at one ‘correct’ design — there isn’t one.

### We WILL grade you on

- **Your judgment about what’s worth building** — and what you chose not to build.
- **How you handled the hard moments** — terms disclosure, decline, late repayment — honestly and humanely.
- **Whether you extended the system coherently and with restraint**, caught what’s wrong in it, and showed your design↔code thinking.
- **How you deliver** — a clean PR against NovaKit Lite is ideal; a runnable repo or deployed link is fine too.
- **The craft on the edges** — error and empty states, micro-interactions, the overall feel of trust.
- **How you drove AI as a partner**, and the quality of what you kept.
- **The clarity and honesty of your written reasoning**, including the three sections above.

## A note on AI use

> We expect you’ll use AI tools to generate, explore, and build — that’s how the job works. Use them however helps you. In the live session we’ll walk through how you built it and the decisions you made, so make sure you understand and can defend everything you submit. Strong candidates use AI to amplify their taste, not replace it — we can usually tell the difference.

## Timeline and the live session

You have 72 hours from when this brief is sent to submit, but this is sized for about 6 hours of focused work — please don’t lose a weekend over it. That’s deliberate: a designer using AI the way this role expects should be able to take this from prompt to a runnable, system-backed build in roughly that time. We care about leverage, not hours logged — if it’s taking dramatically longer, that’s useful signal for both of us.

After we’ve reviewed your submission, you’ll have a 30-minute live session with the hiring manager and one other designer. We’ll click through what you built, ask about your decisions, and probably push back. It’s a discussion, not a defense — we’re trying to understand how you think.
===== PRODUCT_REFERENCE
# NovaPay Salary Advance — Product Reference

A one-page reference so you can focus on design, not on inventing a lending model. Treat these as the rules of the product. Where something isn't specified, make a reasonable assumption and state it.

> NovaPay is a fictional digital wallet used for this exercise. The numbers below are illustrative but internally consistent — design as if they're real.

## What it is

A short-term **salary advance**: a small amount of cash to help a salaried user bridge to their next payday. Short tenor, fixed fee, single repayment pulled on payday.

## Loan tiers

| Tier | Amount (PKR) |
|------|--------------|
| 1 | 5,000 |
| 2 | 10,000 |
| 3 | 15,000 |

A user's offered limit is the highest tier they qualify for. They can take any amount up to that limit (in the tiers above). Requesting more than the offered limit is **not allowed** — that's one of the hard moments you'll design for.

## Cost & repayment

- **Fixed fee** per advance: **3% of the amount disbursed**, charged once (not monthly interest). Example: a Rs 10,000 advance costs Rs 300, so the user repays **Rs 10,300**.
- **Tenor:** repaid in full on the user's **next payday** (assume ~2–4 weeks out; the exact date is known at offer time).
- **Total cost of credit** (amount + fee) and the **repayment date** must be clear at the moment of decision. (See "Trust rules.")
- A "haircut" can apply: the amount actually disbursed may be lower than requested if risk checks warrant it.

## Decisions

- **Approved** — an offer is available; the user can accept.
- **Declined** — no offer. Reasons we surface internally: `credit_score`, `income_unverified`, `other`. How (and how honestly) a decline is communicated to the user is a design decision.
- Income may or may not be **verified** at application (bank statement / payslip). Unverified income is a common decline reason.

## Repayment outcomes (post-disbursement)

- **on_time** — repaid on or before the due date.
- **late** — repaid after the due date (we track days late).
- **default** — 30+ days past due. A user with an active late/overdue advance is a sensitive state to design for (reminders, what they see, tone).

## Trust matters most here

NovaPay operates in a market where predatory digital-lending apps have harmed users and drawn regulatory action — and lending is the highest-trust moment in the whole app. How you earn (or lose) that trust is the heart of this exercise: what you show, when you show it, and how you handle the moments that don't go well. We're deliberately not giving you a checklist — those calls are yours to make and defend.

## Glossary (mirrors the dataset fields, for context)

`applied_amount` · `disbursed_amount` (may be < applied) · `decision` (approved/denied) · `denial_reason` · `repayment_status` (on_time/late/default) · `days_late` · `income_verified` · `income_source` (salaried/freelance).
